summary: Describes an RTP payload format for retransmissions, which recover lost packets in real-time applications with relaxed delay limits. Retransmitted packets are sent in a separate stream from the original, and receivers are assumed to send feedback. It is standards-track.

eli5.summary: If a piece of a live video is lost, the sender sends it again in a separate envelope so the receiver can tell it is a replacement.

questions: what is the rtx payload type
subtitle: How RTP resends lost packets in a separate stream, with the original sequence number tucked inside.

tldr.problem: Lost RTP packets degrade media quality, and simply resending a packet with its old header would corrupt RTCP statistics and hide which packets were lost.
tldr.mechanism: Retransmissions go in a separate RTP stream, either in another session or under another SSRC. Each carries a 2-octet header holding the original sequence number (OSN), then the original payload, and receivers ask for them with RTCP NACK messages.
tldr.outcome: It suits streaming with relaxed delay bounds, for unicast and small multicast groups, and must stay within the congestion budget of the original stream.

today: RFC 4588 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is designed to be used with the RTP/AVPF feedback profile in RFC 4585.

sections.title: When Retransmission Makes Sense
sections.content:
Packet loss between an RTP sender and receiver can degrade media quality. Forward error correction, retransmission and interleaving are all options, and the right choice depends on tolerable latency. For multimedia conferencing the end-to-end delay must be at most a few hundred milliseconds, which usually rules out retransmission. For streaming, an end-to-end delay of several seconds may be acceptable, and that is the target here.

Retransmission trades reliability for delay: endpoints may give up on a packet after a buffering time. Unlike TCP, there is no head-of-line blocking. The method applies to unicast and small multicast groups and is designed for the RTP/AVPF profile (RFC 4585), which allows frequent and early RTCP feedback and defines the NACK message.
sections.eli5: If you are watching a video with a few seconds of cushion, a lost piece can be sent again before you need it. In a live chat there is no time for that.

sections.title: Design Rationale: A Separate Stream
sections.content:
The design must not break RTP and RTCP, must work with mixers, translators and all payload types, and must keep sequence number preservation: the receiver can tell how many and which packets were lost from gaps in sequence numbers.

Two obvious approaches fail. Resending a packet unchanged in the same stream corrupts RTCP statistics, which need the sequence number to rise by one for every packet. Mixing retransmissions into the same stream under a different payload type shares one sequence number space, so the receiver cannot tell which originals were lost. The chosen approach is a separate stream whose packets include the original sequence number.

Two ways to separate the streams are allowed. Session-multiplexing uses two RTP sessions; SSRC-multiplexing uses one session with different SSRC values. Senders and receivers SHOULD support both for unicast, but multicast MUST use session-multiplexing, because associating the streams is problematic otherwise.
sections.eli5: Mixing the re-sent pieces into the normal pile would muddle the numbering. So the re-sent pieces get their own pile, each marked with its original number.

sections.title: The Retransmission Packet
sections.content:
A retransmission packet is an RTP header followed by a 2-octet payload header, the OSN (original sequence number), and then the payload of the original packet, including any payload-specific headers. The RTP header rules are:

  • The sequence number is the ordinary one: one higher than the previous packet in the retransmission stream.
  • The timestamp MUST be the original packet's timestamp, and so its clock rate must match that of the associated original payload type.
  • The payload type is dynamic and mapped through SDP.
  • The marker bit, CSRC count and CSRC list are copied as is. Original padding is removed first.
  • Profile-specific extensions and any header extension SHOULD be repeated, with the payload header placed after them.

With session-multiplexing the same SSRC MUST be used in both streams; with SSRC-multiplexing the two MUST differ. A sender MAY resend data encoded at a lower rate to save bandwidth, as long as receivers can still decode packets that depended on the lost one. Because the retransmission timestamp is the original one, the RTCP jitter value for that stream does not reflect real network jitter.
sections.eli5: The re-sent piece comes in a new envelope, with a small note on top saying which numbered piece it replaces.

sections.title: Associating Streams and Requesting Resends
sections.content:
A retransmission session MUST map to exactly one original session, and a sender MUST use the same RTCP CNAME for a stream and its retransmission stream. With session-multiplexing, the receiver pairs streams that have the same SSRC in the two sessions. With SSRC-multiplexing, it first matches CNAMEs, and when several streams share one it resolves the pairing when a retransmission arrives for a sequence number it requested. To keep this unambiguous, a receiver MUST NOT have two outstanding requests for the same sequence number in two original streams before the association is resolved. That cannot be guaranteed in multicast, so SSRC-multiplexing MUST NOT be used there.

Receivers SHOULD request resends with the AVPF NACK message, and NACKs MUST be sent only for the original stream. A receiver should judge whether a resend would still arrive in time, estimate the round-trip time, and wait a little before asking, in case of reordering. It may re-send a NACK after a timer based on the observed round trip. Sender Reports and BYE packets are handled per stream, and a BYE MUST be sent for both streams. NACKs can go in regular or early RTCP packets, and early packets react faster.
sections.eli5: The receiver has to match each re-sent piece to the right video. It waits a moment before shouting for a missing piece, in case it is merely late, and it only shouts about the original stream.

sections.title: Congestion Control
sections.content: Retransmission can add to congestion, since in a best-effort network loss is caused by congestion. The acceptable packet rate and bitrate include both original and retransmitted data. In a best-effort environment the sender SHOULD NOT send retransmissions without reducing the rate of the original stream, for example by encoding at a lower rate. It MAY retransmit only the packets it deems important and ignore NACKs for others. If congestion is not kept under control, retransmission SHOULD NOT be used. Retransmissions MAY still be sent in some cases, for instance on wireless links where loss is not caused by congestion.
sections.eli5: Re-sending adds more traffic to a road that may already be jammed, so the sender must send less new stuff while re-sending, or only re-send what matters most.

sections.title: SDP Parameters and RTSP
sections.content:
The payload format is registered as MIME subtype rtx for audio, video, text and application. Its required parameters are rate and apt (associated payload type), and an optional rtx-time gives the time in milliseconds a sender keeps a packet available for retransmission. They go in SDP as a=fmtp:<number> apt=<apt-value>;rtx-time=<rtx-time-val>.

With session-multiplexing, the SDP MUST group the original and retransmission m lines with FID semantics, except when there is exactly one of each. With SSRC-multiplexing, one m line lists both payload types. For RTSP, the retransmission stream SHOULD NOT be controlled by PLAY and PAUSE, and it SHOULD NOT be cached.
sections.eli5: The call's info card says which re-send format goes with which normal format and how long the sender keeps old pieces around.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The general RTP security considerations apply. Without authentication, tampered RTCP could trigger inappropriate retransmissions that eat into the original stream's bitrate, tampered retransmission packets could crash a decoder, and replayed packets could distort RTT measurements and overflow the receiver buffer. To keep data confidential the original payload must be encrypted; the 2-byte payload header need not be.

If the original stream is protected, the same services at equivalent strength MUST be provided on the retransmission stream. Using the same key for both may lead to two-time pads. The RFC notes that SRTP of the time did not provide all of this, partly because it supported RTP/AVP while this format usually runs under RTP/AVPF.
sections.eli5: If the original is locked, the re-sent copy needs an equally good lock, and not the same key, or a snoop could compare the two.
